name: Jade Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no links to employers, AI companies, unions or government. What you say is confidential. What happens on a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and became a team manager in the appointment office of a large medical equipment company this year. Six coordinators book repairs for clinics, check warranty dates and answer calls when a breathing machine is waiting for a part. I came up through customer service and have a bachelor’s degree, but I am still slow at the manager reports and sometimes miss a staffing clash. I use AI tools every day to draft plans and spot double bookings, then ask a coordinator to check before anything goes to a clinic.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are the pressures at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives a local bus, and our children are seven and eleven. We have a mortgage and less than a month of expenses in savings. My manager salary is low because I am new to the job, and there are few offices like this nearby. I like testing a new tool, but I cannot test our mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau is familiar territory for our office. We can let a tool draft an appointment note, but a coordinator still needs to make sure a clinic has a repair slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I am already worried about money. The bus company has changed my partner’s shifts twice this year, and one lost week would take most of our savings. Even a small automation could mean they do not replace a coordinator, leaving me with more calls to cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the daily check of clinic bookings and use my current AI calendar to flag double appointments. If a new routine tool arrives, I’d test it with last month’s missed visits before approving it. We would move the children’s paid music lessons to the cheaper group class next term if the budget stays tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. The tool is small, but our mortgage and shifting bus hours are not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with a missed visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A technician arrived at a clinic while the nurse was on a ward round. The system showed “confirmed,” but no one had asked the nurse about the time. I called back and found a later slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children mind the group class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our youngest would complain about losing one-to-one time. I would explain that we are keeping music, just changing the cost. My partner and I would make the choice together after seeing next month’s shifts.

say: **AI Plateau** changes only routine notes in our office.
A coordinator must still confirm a **real repair slot** with the clinic.
think: The **mortgage** and changing bus shifts already make us vulnerable.
Even small automation could leave an unfilled **coordinator vacancy**.
do: **Keep** daily checks of clinic bookings in 2026.
**Test** a new routine tool on last month’s missed visits.
**Move** the children to group music lessons if the budget stays tight.
feel: I feel **anxious** about mortgage and bus hours despite limited AI change.
S0.quote: The system showed “confirmed,” but no one had asked the nurse about the time.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** does not remove existing financial worry from a thin cushion and uncertain bus shifts.
She treats a **missed clinic visit** as a time and care problem, not a calendar score.

steps.text: Keep checking clinic repair bookings with coordinators each morning
Test the new tool on last month missed clinic visits
Move children to group music lessons if next month budget stays tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the coordinators Steady Disruption will write notes, book visits, check warranties and answer many simple calls. We should use the change to give clinics a clearer way to reach a person when a repair is urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the booking and checking work can move to software. I am new at managing people, so I may be easier to replace than an experienced lead. Our household cannot carry a pay cut for long, and there are few other offices nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d put our missed repair visits into the company’s AI pilot and compare what it books with the nurse’s actual availability. I’d take the paid system-training session if my director offers me a place, then show the coordinators what I learnt. If the team loses hours, we’d stop the children’s music lessons for a term while I apply for any open service-supervisor jobs that meet our mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can learn quickly, but being quick with a tool may not keep a junior manager post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a clinic need to reach a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clinic needs a number answered by someone who can move a technician, not a form that sends an email tomorrow. Last Friday a clinic had patients waiting and a broken part on the bench. I moved another visit and found a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle the music decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children it is a pause, not a punishment. Our eleven-year-old would ask if my job was gone. I would answer honestly that my hours might change, then look at free music sessions nearby.

say: **Bookings and checks** will change, but urgent clinics need a live answer.
I’d test AI visits against **nurse availability**.
think: My **junior manager post** may be easier to cut than an experienced lead’s.
A **pay cut** would put our mortgage at risk quickly.
do: **Test** missed visits in the company AI pilot this month.
**Take** paid system training if the director offers a place.
**Apply** for service-supervisor openings only if pay covers the mortgage.
feel: I feel **alarmed** that tool skill may not protect this new post.
S1.quote: A clinic needs a number answered by someone who can move a technician, not a form that sends an email tomorrow.
fieldNote: She acts early with a **pilot** while privately seeing her new manager post as vulnerable.
The **music pause** is a specific household response if hours fall, not a prediction that lessons are already gone.
She says **alarmed**, but describes a possible cut rather than a certain loss of her own income.

steps.text: Test missed repair visits in the company AI pilot
Take paid system training if the director offers a place
Apply for service-supervisor openings only if pay covers the mortgage
Pause children music lessons for one term if work hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office AGI by 2028 could do nearly all our booking, checking and customer replies. We need dates for staffing decisions and a human line for clinics when machines are down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI in 2028 could take my desk work before robots can do hands-on repairs around 2031. I expect most of our appointment office to shrink, and I think my new manager role is likely to be cut. My partner’s bus wage would not cover the mortgage and two children on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d ask the director for the staffing schedule and ask payroll for the real severance amount. My partner and I would check our monthly bills, cancel streaming and the planned weekend trip in 2027 to hold cash, and call the mortgage lender for payment options before we miss one. In 2027 I’d apply for the open clinic liaison post if the salary covers mortgage and school costs; if AGI arrives in 2028 and I’m cut, I’d take a confirmed offer, not count on a vacancy still existing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. My mind goes straight to the mortgage due date, but I can still make the calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the streaming services and skip the planned weekend trip in 2027. Cancelling streaming and a weekend trip would help with groceries but not replace my salary. I would keep the children’s school transport paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a clinic liaison doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taking the difficult repair calls and checking what the clinic actually needs. I have done parts of it, but the posted role asks for more equipment knowledge. I would speak to its manager before applying, and I would not say it is safe from AI.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs staffing dates and a human repair line for clinics.
I would ask for the real **severance amount**.
think: My office thinking work could go in **2028**, before repair robots around 2031.
My new post is **likely to be cut**; one bus wage cannot cover our bills.
do: **Ask** the director and payroll tomorrow for dates and severance.
**Cancel** streaming and the planned weekend trip in 2027 to hold cash.
**Apply** in 2027 for clinic liaison only if pay covers mortgage and school costs.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the mortgage due date, though I can make practical calls.
S2.quote: Cancelling streaming and a weekend trip would help with groceries but not replace my salary.
fieldNote: She expects **her post** to end and has less than a month of savings.
Her **liaison application** depends on salary and learning equipment details, while the lender call is only a request for options.

steps.text: Apply for clinic liaison vacancy if salary covers mortgage and school costs
Cancel streaming and planned weekend trip in 2027 to hold cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to train coordinators for work closer to clinics. A plan has to include paid hours, not a link to a course after a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My booking screens could still be taken by AGI around 2031, while robots that do repairs arrive around 2034. Five years lets me build equipment knowledge before applying elsewhere, but I cannot assume our company will fund every course or keep a liaison vacancy open. The mortgage still needs the full payment each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning in January 2027 I’d spend one paid afternoon a month with a field-service coordinator if both managers approve cover. I’d take the equipment certificate if the company funds it and gives me paid study time. Once AGI arrives in 2031, I’d apply for a clinic liaison role only if a real vacancy pays enough for our mortgage and school transport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. More time gives me a route, but the route must come with wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on a field afternoon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which spare parts can wait and which device must be fixed before a patient comes back. I know the appointment board, not the inside of the machine. I would carry a notebook and ask the technician to correct my guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the certificate is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep doing the paid field afternoons if approved and look at a free basic course, but I would not claim that makes me qualified. We cannot pay for a costly certificate from this month’s bills. I would try again when an employer offers a funded place.

say: **Five years** could build paid paths closer to clinic work.
Training must happen in **paid hours**, not after a full shift.
think: Booking work faces AGI in **2031**, before repair robots around 2034.
A funded course and **liaison vacancy** are both uncertain.
do: **Shadow** field service monthly from January 2027 if cover is approved.
**Take** the equipment certificate only with funding and paid study time.
**Apply** after 2031 only for liaison work covering mortgage and school transport.
feel: I feel **anxious** because the route depends on wages and an opening.
S3.quote: I know the appointment board, not the inside of the machine.
fieldNote: She identifies a **specific equipment gap** despite using AI daily for office tasks.
The **paid field trial** and certificate are conditional because the household cannot fund a costly course.

steps.text: Shadow field service monthly if both managers approve paid cover
Take equipment certificate only with company funding and paid study time
Apply for liaison vacancy after 2031 only if pay covers mortgage and school transport

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives employers enough years to make a real training ladder. I would ask for a clear list of paid clinic-facing jobs, what each pays and how coordinators can qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years our children will be older, and if our wages hold we might have paid down the mortgage and saved a little more. My booking and reporting work could still be replaced by thinking AI in 2036; robots for hands-on repairs come around 2039. I would not treat a long runway as job security, but it lets me learn while employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep using the AI calendar and keep reviewing missed appointments with coordinators. I’d set aside a small amount from each full-pay month for an emergency fund only after the mortgage and school costs clear, and I’d take a paid clinic liaison rotation if the company offers it without a wage cut. After 2036 I’d seek a clinic operations job only if the actual pay keeps the mortgage current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than alarmed. Ten years could give us a cushion and a better skill, if the pay keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How small is the savings amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe fifteen in a month when all my partner’s bus shifts run. I would put fifteen into a separate emergency account after the monthly mortgage payment and school costs clear, not promise it before payday. If school costs rise, we would skip a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the training ladder show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posted wage, the equipment knowledge needed and who covers the office while a coordinator learns. I have seen a course listed with no opening at the end. I would ask for a real job attached.

say: A **decade** should bring posted clinic jobs and paid training steps.
A course should lead toward a **real opening**.
think: We might reduce the **mortgage** and save if both wages hold.
Booking faces AGI in **2036**, before repair robots around 2039.
do: **Keep** checking missed appointments with coordinators in 2026.
**Save** fifteen in full-pay months after the mortgage and school costs clear.
**Take** a paid clinic liaison rotation if offered without a wage cut.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with a possible route if wages continue.
S4.quote: I would put fifteen into a separate emergency account after the monthly mortgage payment and school costs clear, not promise it before payday.
fieldNote: Her **long runway** allows conditional saving, but full bus shifts and school costs still decide each month.
She wants a **posted wage** and office cover before calling a course a career path.

steps.text: Keep checking missed clinic appointments with coordinators
Save fifteen in full-pay months after mortgage and school costs clear
Take paid clinic liaison rotation if offered without a wage cut
Seek clinic operations job after 2036 only if pay keeps mortgage current

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the appointment office could shrink before I can learn the equipment side. A clear cut date, a funded certificate and a real liaison vacancy with a posted wage would help. The mortgage will not wait for me to finish a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask a clinic nurse what a missed repair visit does to the day. A calendar can be perfectly filled and still leave a patient waiting for a working machine. Someone needs to own that call.

headlineQuote: A calendar can be perfectly filled and still leave a patient waiting for a working machine.
portrait: **Jade, 43**, is a recently promoted appointment-office manager at a large medical equipment company with a bachelor’s degree.
Her **low pay**, two school-age children, mortgage and under-one-month reserve make lost hours dangerous.
She uses **AI daily** to draft plans but still checks clinic timing with coordinators and is learning manager reports.
She is **anxious** even in AI Plateau, expects fast desk cuts and seeks funded clinic-facing work with wage protection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her new manager post before she learns enough equipment work.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **cut date**, funded certificate and posted liaison wage would help her decide.
